title: Rework
author: Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson

lessons.title: Ignore the So-Called Real World
lessons.key_idea: The warnings people give about how business 'really works' are mostly excuses, and you can build something on your own saner terms.

lessons.title: Plans Are Just Guesses
lessons.key_idea: Long-term business plans pretend to predict an unknowable future, so it's smarter to decide what to do next based on what you know now.

lessons.title: Scratch Your Own Itch
lessons.key_idea: The best products come from solving a problem you have yourself, and ideas mean little until you actually start making something.

lessons.title: Constraints Are Your Hidden Advantage
lessons.key_idea: Having less money, time and people forces you to find simpler, more creative solutions than well-funded competitors.

lessons.title: Build Half a Product, Not a Bad One
lessons.key_idea: Cut features ruthlessly so you can do a small number of things really well, and make saying no your default.

lessons.title: Meetings and Interruptions Kill Real Work
lessons.key_idea: Real work needs long stretches of uninterrupted time, so protect your team from needless meetings and constant pings.

lessons.title: Launch Now, Work Calmly, Keep It Simple
lessons.key_idea: Good enough shipped today beats perfect someday, and a lean, sustainable pace beats heroic overwork every time.

plan.title: Rework
plan.author: Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's main arguments and chapter themes well, though I would avoid quoting exact wording or minor anecdotes.
plan.one_liner: Most business advice is wrong. Here's a simpler, calmer, smaller way to build something that works.
plan.summary: Rework is a short, punchy manifesto from the founders of 37signals, the company behind Basecamp. They argue that much of the conventional wisdom about starting and running a business is outdated or simply wrong. You don't need outside investors, a detailed business plan, a big team, or eighty-hour weeks. Instead, they urge readers to start small, build something they personally need, and treat limits on time, money and people as advantages. They champion cutting features until only the essential core remains, launching before things feel perfect, and saying no far more often than yes. They also take aim at workplace habits that quietly destroy productivity, especially meetings and constant interruptions. The result is a practical, contrarian guide to doing better work with less stress, less waste and far less ceremony.
